newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition backs French EU jobs drive.
newsitem.headline: German opposition backs French EU jobs drive.

text.p: Germany's opposition, seizing on France's bid to make job creation a European Union priority, on Wednesday attacked the Bonn government for neglecting the fight against record post-war unemployment to pursue the grail of monetary union.

Social Democrat (SPD) and Greens speakers strongly backed the call by the new left-wing government in Paris to add a jobs chapter to the so-called Maastricht II treaty reforming the EU which is due to be signed next week at a summit in Amsterdam.

They also said Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel's new-found readiness to sign up to an employment chapter in the treaty clashed with the record of a government which has failed to act while German unemployment climbed over four million.

"After you, the government, said for months that a jobs chapter was irrelevant because employment policy should be 'home-made', you now find yourselves completely isolated," SPD European affairs spokeswoman Heidemarie Wieczorek-Zeul said.

Wieczorek-Zeul, speaking in a parliamentary debate on the June 16-17 Amsterdam summit expected to finalise the treaty, said Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government was still trying to water down the jobs pact.
Waving a blank piece of paper, she said: "These are the government's proposals for the employment chapter...Your contribution consists only of deletions...a zero proposal".
She added that the SPD -- which has the power to block ratification of Maastricht II in the upper house of parliament -- would only vote for a substantive jobs chapter.
Earlier in the debate, Kinkel said he was prepared to agree to the employment chapter as long as it did not create wasteful job creation schemes or cost Germany any money.
The Bundestag lower house of parliament passed, by a show of hands, a motion by Kohl's centre-right coalition insisting that it would not agree to any extra spending on job schemes.

Opposition speakers said the resolution smacked of the type of "neo-liberal" policies which had forced up unemployment in Germany and thrown Finance Minister Theo Waigel's effort to hit borrowing targets to qualify for the euro currency off course.
"Theo Waigel wants to make a monetary straitjacket for the European Union which the people reject," Wieczorek-Zeul said.
"We must cut the European coat so that it fits the people."
Greens European spokesman Christian Sterzing agreed: "The democratic deficit at European level is just like the budget deficit at the national level.
"We want the euro, but we don't want it as an instrument of neo-liberal policy," he said. "Open yourself to the new mood coming from France, and support a substantial jobs chapter."

Recent opinion polls show the two opposition parties with a clear lead over the 14-year-old Kohl coalition, raising the prospect of a 'red-green' coalition taking power after the general election due in October 1998.
